1.point: The dead do not go anywhere; this chapter shows why by setting out the soul and its worlds in four steps.
steps: Open on the prayer's image of sleep as neglect before the meeting with God
Move from sleep to death and the common picture of barzakh as a distant waiting room
State the counter-claim (at death we don't go anywhere), ground it in the soul, and name the four steps the chapter takes

2.point: Creation has three nested worlds (matter, images, intellects) and the deeper two are dimensions of this one, not distant places.
steps: The soul is a compact copy of creation, so it can serve as a map of creation
The soul knows in three ways, so it holds three kinds of thing, so creation has three worlds
Senses meet matter: the material world
Imagination holds shaped, colourless-of-matter images: the world of images, which exists outside any mind
Intellect grasps pure meanings: the world of intellects
The world of images stands between the other two (barzakh), so the worlds are ordered one inside another
The unseen worlds are deeper dimensions of this world, not places far away

3.point: Whenever the body's hold on the soul loosens the soul enters the world of images; at death the hold ends and the soul stays there in an image body.
steps: The soul stands between spirit and body, so it touches matter and can enter the middle world
Normally the body's hold on the soul's attention keeps it in the material world; that hold loosens at three times
In sleep the hold slackens and the soul touches the world of images (hence dreams of the future)
Death is the same loosening carried to completion: the soul lets the body go and continues in the image body
In watchfulness a person loosens the hold deliberately and sees the same world
So barzakh at the graveside is the world of images, a deeper dimension of this world, not a distant room

4.point: Unlike a fixed angel the soul can be shaped; repeated deeds shape it, and the form it has at death is the form it meets in the middle world.
steps: Angels have fixed stations and do not change
The human soul has no fixed station, so it can be shaped by the life it lives
Repeated acts become habits and habits become part of the soul
The shaping shows faintly on the face but strongly on the image body
The form the soul has when it leaves the body is the form it keeps in the next world
Rewards and punishments are the deeds themselves made manifest, so every deed has a reality in the middle world

5.point: The one self passes through three states by changing its attitude, and the means of change are in our hands, with God's mercy supplying the start.
steps: The Qur'an gives the self three names, read as three states of one self
The commanding self: bodily side wins; God's mercy is what lifts it
The blaming self: remorse shows that values outrank pleasure
The self at peace: free of sin, greed and bodily preoccupation
These are one self under three names, so changing the attitude changes the state
Familiar acts change the attitude: remembrance brings the rest of the third state; fasting and night prayer loosen the body's hold
The change lasts because the soul takes on habits; the soul is entrusted to us and what we make of it remains
Therefore what the soul becomes is, by God's grace, in our hands

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: Explains the opening quotation and supplies the hook: sleep as a picture of neglect set beside the meeting with God.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Moves from sleep to death and states the common picture (barzakh as a far-off waiting room) that the chapter will overturn.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: States the thesis ('we don't go anywhere'), grounds it in the soul, and lays out the four steps the chapter takes.

¶4.label: advance
¶4.why: Supplies the method: the soul is a compact copy of creation, so its contents map creation's worlds.

¶5.label: advance
¶5.why: Three ways of knowing give three kinds of thing and so three worlds; sets up the next three paragraphs.

¶6.label: advance
¶6.why: First world: the senses meet matter; introduces witnessed vs unseen.

¶7.label: advance
¶7.why: Second world: the imagination's shaped but matterless things; the world of images exists outside any mind.

¶8.label: advance
¶8.why: Third world: pure meanings grasped by the intellect; angels as pure intellect (used again in Section 4).

¶9.label: advance
¶9.why: Supplies the ordering: the world of images stands between the others, which is why it is barzakh and why the worlds nest. The closing sentence on kursi, 'arsh and jabarut is an aside the section never uses and should go.

¶10.label: advance
¶10.why: Supplies the second half of the point: the worlds are not far away but deeper dimensions of this one.

¶11.label: support
¶11.why: Imam 'Ali's answer and the hell verse give evidence for the nesting and 'not far away' claims of ¶9-¶10; ¶12's 'one inside another' draws on it.

¶12.label: restate
¶12.why: Summarises the section; every claim was made in ¶5-¶10.

¶13.label: advance
¶13.why: Explains why the soul can enter the middle world: it stands between spirit and body as the world of images stands between intellect and matter. The sentences on God having no parts and the Ka'ba are a side remark within an otherwise needed paragraph.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: Introduces the body's hold on the soul and names the three times it loosens; the frame for ¶15-¶20.

¶15.label: advance
¶15.why: First loosening: sleep lets the soul touch the world of images; the future-dream point shows it is that world and not memory.

¶16.label: advance
¶16.why: Introduces the second loosening and the verse that pairs death with sleep. Thin: two sentences that could open ¶17.

¶17.label: support
¶17.why: Shomali's reading of the verse supplies the 'difference of degree' that ¶18 and ¶20 rely on to treat sleep and death as one hold at two depths.

¶18.label: advance
¶18.why: Death as the complete letting go and the image body as what the soul continues in; this is the 'at death it stays there' step.

¶19.label: advance
¶19.why: Third loosening: watchfulness does on purpose what sleep does; the Tabataba'i remark is evidence for it.

¶20.label: restate
¶20.why: Summarises ¶15-¶19; nothing new, the point is already in hand.

¶21.label: advance
¶21.why: Draws the graveside consequence: barzakh of the dead is the world of images, so the dead have gone deeper, not away. New link, though it reaches past the section's point to the chapter's.

¶22.label: advance
¶22.why: Angels have a fixed station and do not change; the contrast the point requires.

¶23.label: advance
¶23.why: The soul has no fixed place and is shaped by the life it lives; the Adam remark supports this.

¶24.label: advance
¶24.why: How the shaping happens: repetition, habit, and the lying example that carries it.

¶25.label: advance
¶25.why: Where the shaping shows: faintly on the face, strongly on the image body; needed for 'meets that shape in the middle world'.

¶26.label: advance
¶26.why: The form at departure is the form kept in the next world; Khomeini supplies the step that fixes when the shape is settled.

¶27.label: aside
¶27.why: Introduces Surah al-Naba' as a second witness to the step ¶26 already established; nothing later uses the groups coming forth. ¶28's first sentence goes with it.

¶28.label: support
¶28.why: Introduces the al-Hadid light verse that ¶29 reads and ¶30 builds on; its first sentence only repeats ¶26 via al-Naba'.

¶29.label: support
¶29.why: Reads the light as the faithful's own piety shining; ¶30's opening conditional uses exactly this reading. The aside that the Last Day body is not the image body raises a complication and does not resolve it.

¶30.label: advance
¶30.why: New step: rewards are the deeds themselves made manifest, so each deed has a reality in the middle world; also sets up the Ibn 'Arabi box.

¶31.label: restate
¶31.why: States the section's conclusion but every element is already on the page: deeds shape the image body (¶25), deeds have images in barzakh (¶30). 'Our future is now present' is a tidy aphorism closing the section.

¶32.label: advance
¶32.why: Introduces the nafs, its three names read as three states, and the ascending order the section follows.

¶33.label: advance
¶33.why: First state, the commanding self, with the Yusuf verse that names the mercy that lifts it.

¶34.label: advance
¶34.why: Two new links: God's mercy is what overcomes the commanding self (used in ¶43 for 'by God's grace'), and worry binds the soul to the body (used in ¶42 'trained to worry about the body').

¶35.label: advance
¶35.why: Second state, the blaming self, and why self-blame is hopeful; the step from first to second.

¶36.label: advance
¶36.why: Third state, the self at peace, reached by keeping up self-blame.

¶37.label: advance
¶37.why: The hinge of the section: one self, three attitudes, so the state can be changed.

¶38.label: advance
¶38.why: Supplies that familiar acts change the attitude and names the two to be shown. Thin: a two-sentence signpost that could open ¶39.

¶39.label: advance
¶39.why: First means: remembrance of God; introduces the Ra'd verse.

¶40.label: support
¶40.why: The shared root of the verse's 'rest' and mutma'inna ties remembrance to the third state; without it ¶39 would not connect to ¶36.

¶41.label: advance
¶41.why: Second means: fasting and night prayer loosen the body's hold, which is what makes the self command to evil; links back to Section 3.

¶42.label: advance
¶42.why: The change lasts because the soul takes on habits, and the soul is entrusted to us for a time; this is the 'in our hands' step.

¶43.label: restate
¶43.why: Summarises the whole chapter section by section. Its one new link, that the drive to begin is God's mercy from Surah Yusuf, belongs in ¶42 or a single closing sentence; the rest repeats ¶12, ¶20, ¶31 and ¶37.

¶44.label: aside
¶44.why: A new question the chapter does not answer, raised as a teaser for the next chapter; the point is already landed.
